title: Psychophysics: Measuring the Mind
description: How sensory magnitudes map to physical stimuli, and how decisions are made under noise

concepts.title: Weber's Law and the Just-Noticeable Difference
concepts.contentHtml:
Psychophysics, founded by Gustav Fechner in Elemente der Psychophysik (1860), is the study of how physical stimuli are translated into subjective experience. Its first quantitative law was discovered by Ernst Weber.

Weber's law states that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus — the just-noticeable difference (JND) — is a constant fraction of the baseline stimulus. If you can just detect a 1g addition to a 100g weight, you will need a 10g addition to detect change in a 1000g weight.

Formally: ΔI / I = k, where I is the reference intensity, ΔI is the JND, and k is the Weber fraction (about 0.02 for line length, 0.10 for loudness). Weber fractions are a fingerprint of each sensory channel.

The law captures something deep: perception is sensitive to relative rather than absolute change. A whisper in silence is striking; the same whisper in a busy market is unheard.

concepts.title: Fechner and Stevens: Two Laws of Sensation
concepts.contentHtml:
Fechner integrated Weber's law to derive a relationship between physical intensity and subjective sensation. His logarithmic law: S = k log(I/I₀), where S is sensation, I is intensity, and I₀ is the absolute threshold. Doubling a stimulus does not double the sensation — equal ratios produce equal increments of experience.

A century later, S.S. Stevens (1957) challenged Fechner using magnitude estimation: ask listeners to assign numbers proportional to perceived loudness. The data fit a power law better than a logarithmic one: S = k Iⁿ.

The exponent n varies by modality: about 0.33 for brightness, 0.67 for loudness, 1.0 for line length, and 3.5 for electric shock. Exponents below 1 compress: huge changes in light produce small changes in brightness, useful given the enormous range of natural illumination. Exponents above 1 expand: small increases in shock feel disproportionately worse, useful as a danger signal.

concepts.title: Signal Detection Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical psychophysics treated thresholds as fixed boundaries, but signal detection theory (Tanner and Swets, 1954) reframes detection as a decision under noise.

On every trial, neural activity arises from either noise alone or signal-plus-noise. Both produce overlapping distributions of internal evidence. The observer adopts a criterion: respond 'yes' when evidence exceeds it. This generates four outcomes: hits, misses, false alarms, correct rejections.

Two parameters separate sensitivity from bias. d-prime (d′) measures the distance between the noise and signal distributions in standard-deviation units — pure perceptual sensitivity, independent of strategy. The criterion (c) measures decision bias: a conservative observer demands more evidence before saying 'yes', sacrificing hits to reduce false alarms.

Signal detection theory revolutionised perception research. It explained why an anxious radar operator misses targets while a confident one cries wolf — both can be equally sensitive but differ in criterion. It is now standard across psychology, medical diagnosis, and machine learning.

title: The Visual System
description: From photons at the retina to recognition in cortex

concepts.title: Retina: Rods, Cones, and Centre-Surround
concepts.contentHtml:
Vision begins in the retina, a thin sheet of neural tissue at the back of the eye. Two classes of photoreceptor convert light into electrical signals.

Rods (about 120 million per retina) are exquisitely sensitive — a single photon can trigger a response — but they are achromatic and pool over wide areas, sacrificing spatial detail for sensitivity. They dominate scotopic (night) vision and are absent from the central fovea.

Cones (about 6 million) come in three types tuned to short, medium, and long wavelengths. They are densely packed in the fovea, support sharp daytime vision, and provide colour. Outside the fovea, acuity drops sharply: peripheral vision is far blurrier than introspection suggests.

Retinal ganglion cells already perform sophisticated processing. Their centre-surround receptive fields (Kuffler, 1953) respond to local contrast, not absolute light. This is why uniform illumination fades from awareness while edges are emphasised — the retina is an edge detector, not a passive camera.

concepts.title: Hubel and Wiesel: Feature Detectors in V1
concepts.contentHtml:
In a series of experiments beginning in 1959, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel recorded from single neurons in the cat primary visual cortex (V1) and discovered cells that respond selectively to oriented edges.

Simple cells respond to a bar of light at a specific orientation in a specific position. Complex cells respond to the same orientation across a larger region, achieving translation invariance. Hypercomplex (end-stopped) cells respond best to bars of a particular length.

Hubel and Wiesel mapped the columnar organisation of V1: nearby neurons share preferences for orientation and eye dominance, organised in regular tiled patterns. They also showed that depriving a kitten of vision in one eye during a critical period permanently rewired its cortex — a dramatic demonstration of experience-dependent plasticity.

The work, awarded the 1981 Nobel Prize, established the principle that perception is built up by hierarchies of feature detectors, each combining the outputs of simpler ones — an architecture later inspiring convolutional neural networks.

concepts.title: Two Streams: What and Where
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond V1, visual information splits into two cortical pathways, identified by Ungerleider and Mishkin (1982).

The ventral stream runs from V1 through V4 into inferior temporal cortex. It is the 'what' pathway: it computes object identity, faces, scenes, and colour. Damage produces visual agnosias — patients see clearly but cannot recognise. Prosopagnosia (face blindness) follows lesions to the fusiform face area.

The dorsal stream runs from V1 through V5/MT into posterior parietal cortex. It is the 'where' or 'how' pathway: it computes location, motion, and the spatial guidance of action. Damage produces optic ataxia: patients can describe an object but cannot reach for it accurately.

Milner and Goodale's revision frames it as vision-for-perception versus vision-for-action. Patient D.F., with ventral damage, could not report the orientation of a slot but could post a card through it without difficulty: action and awareness rely on partly separate visual systems.

title: Organisation, Depth, and Colour
description: Gestalt grouping, the cues we use to see in 3D, and how the brain constructs colour

concepts.title: Gestalt Principles of Grouping
concepts.contentHtml:
Early 20th-century Gestalt psychologists — Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler, and Kurt Koffka — argued that perception is not built additively from local features. The whole is organised by principles that group elements into coherent units.

Proximity: elements close together are seen as a group. Similarity: elements that share colour, size, or shape are grouped. Closure: gaps in a contour are filled in to form a complete figure — three Pac-Man shapes evoke an illusory triangle (Kanizsa). Common fate: elements moving together are grouped, even when stationary they would not be.

Good continuation: contours are extended along smooth paths. Figure-ground: at any moment one region is foreground, another background — a bistable distinction in the Rubin vase.

The Gestaltists captured genuine regularities, though their explanatory framework (field forces in the brain) has been replaced. Their principles are now understood as priors the visual system uses to solve the inverse problem of inferring scenes from images.

concepts.title: Depth: Binocular and Monocular Cues
concepts.contentHtml:
The retinal image is two-dimensional, yet we perceive a 3D world. The brain combines many cues.

Binocular disparity: the two eyes view the scene from slightly different positions, producing horizontal offsets between matching points. The brain solves this correspondence problem and converts disparity into depth — the basis of stereoscopic vision and 3D films. Bela Julesz's random-dot stereograms (1960) showed disparity alone, with no monocular cues, suffices for vivid depth.

Monocular (pictorial) cues work in a single eye and are the painter's tools: linear perspective (parallel lines converge), occlusion (nearer objects hide farther ones), relative size, texture gradient (texture compresses with distance), aerial perspective (distant objects look hazier), and shading (light from above is a default assumption).

Motion parallax: as you move, near objects sweep across the visual field faster than far ones. This dynamic cue is powerful enough that structure-from-motion reveals 3D shape from a moving cloud of dots that is meaningless when static.

concepts.title: Colour: Trichromacy, Opponent Process, and Retinex
concepts.contentHtml:
Three theories of colour, once thought to compete, are now known to describe successive stages of the same system.

Trichromatic theory (Young, 1802; Helmholtz, 1850s): the retina contains three cone types — short (S), medium (M), long (L). Any colour is encoded by the relative activity of the three. This explains why three primaries suffice to mix any visible hue and why dichromats lack one cone type.

Opponent-process theory (Hering, 1892): we never experience reddish-green or bluish-yellow. Hering proposed three opponent channels — red vs green, blue vs yellow, black vs white. Hurvich and Jameson (1957) confirmed cones feed into opponent ganglion cells: red-green is L−M, blue-yellow is S−(L+M). Negative afterimages follow naturally from channel adaptation.

Land's Retinex theory (1977) addresses colour constancy: a banana looks yellow under blue noon light or warm tungsten light, even though the wavelengths reaching the eye differ enormously. The visual system estimates the illuminant and discounts it, recovering surface reflectance. Colour is not in the light but in the relations the brain computes across the scene.

title: Audition and Multisensory Integration
description: How the cochlea encodes sound, how we localise it, and how the senses combine

concepts.title: The Cochlea and Frequency Coding
concepts.contentHtml:
The cochlea is a coiled fluid-filled tube that performs a biomechanical Fourier analysis of sound. The basilar membrane running along its length varies systematically in stiffness and width: it is narrow and stiff at the base, wide and floppy at the apex.

High-frequency sounds set up travelling waves that peak near the base; low-frequency sounds peak near the apex. Place coding (Georg von Békésy, 1961 Nobel Prize) means each frequency stimulates hair cells at a particular location, which feed corresponding fibres in the auditory nerve. The cochlea is tonotopically organised, and so are auditory cortex maps that mirror it.

For low frequencies (below about 4 kHz), neurons can also fire in synchrony with the waveform itself — temporal coding via phase locking. The auditory system uses both: place dominates at high frequencies, timing at low. Damage to hair cells produces sensorineural hearing loss; cochlear implants exploit place coding by stimulating different electrode positions to mimic frequency.

concepts.title: Sound Localisation
concepts.contentHtml:
To locate a sound source, the brain compares the signals at the two ears — but the cues differ depending on frequency.

Interaural time differences (ITDs): a sound from the right reaches the right ear roughly 600 microseconds before the left. Neurons in the medial superior olive act as coincidence detectors (Jeffress model, 1948), firing maximally when inputs from the two ears arrive simultaneously after compensating delays. ITDs are most useful below about 1.5 kHz, where wavelengths are larger than head width and there is no phase ambiguity.

Interaural level differences (ILDs): high-frequency sounds are partly blocked (the 'acoustic shadow') by the head, so the far ear receives a quieter signal. The lateral superior olive computes these differences and dominates at high frequencies.

Front-back and up-down disambiguation rely on spectral cues from the pinna's filtering — the head-related transfer function. Owls use asymmetric ears for 2D localisation; humans tilt their heads to break ambiguity.

concepts.title: Multisensory Integration
concepts.contentHtml:
Perception rarely uses one sense at a time. The brain combines vision, hearing, touch, and proprioception to estimate the world more reliably than any single channel could.

The McGurk effect (McGurk and MacDonald, 1976) is dramatic: hearing 'ba' while watching lips say 'ga' yields a perception of 'da'. Speech perception is fundamentally audiovisual, not auditory.

The ventriloquist effect shows visual capture of sound location: if a puppet's mouth moves, voices appear to come from it, not the speaker. Vision dominates because it provides more precise spatial information than audition.

Ernst and Banks (2002) showed multisensory combination is approximately statistically optimal: the brain weights each cue by its reliability, like a Bayesian observer. When vision is blurred, touch dominates a size estimate; when touch is noisy, vision dominates. The rubber hand illusion (Botvinick and Cohen, 1998) — feeling ownership of a fake hand stroked in synchrony with your hidden real one — shows even body ownership is a multisensory inference, not a fixed fact.

title: Illusions and the Predictive Brain
description: What illusions reveal about top-down inference and predictive coding

concepts.title: Geometric Illusions
concepts.contentHtml:
Illusions are not failures of perception but exposures of the assumptions perception relies on.

In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two equal-length lines look unequal because of the arrowheads at their ends — outward fins make a line appear longer than inward ones. Richard Gregory proposed the brain interprets the fins as depth cues (an inside corner versus an outside corner) and applies size-distance scaling: a line apparently farther away must be longer to project the same retinal image. Cross-cultural work (Segall, 1966) found the illusion is weaker for people raised in less rectilinear environments.

The Ponzo illusion works similarly: identical bars over converging rails look unequal, because the converging lines suggest perspective. The Ames room uses a cleverly distorted shape that produces the same retinal image as a normal room, making one occupant look gigantic and another tiny.

These illusions show perception is inference: the brain uses learned regularities about the world to interpret ambiguous images, and these heuristics misfire when stimuli violate the assumptions they were tuned for.

concepts.title: Change Blindness and Attention
concepts.contentHtml:
Introspection suggests we see the world in rich, detailed colour everywhere. Experiments show otherwise.

Change blindness (Rensink, 1997): if a brief flicker masks the moment of change, observers fail to notice large alterations to a scene — a building disappearing, a sky changing colour. Inattentional blindness (Simons and Chabris, 1999): viewers counting basketball passes routinely miss a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene.

Motion-induced blindness: bright stationary dots can vanish from awareness when surrounded by a moving pattern, then reappear. Even vivid stimuli can drop out of consciousness when attention is diverted.

These phenomena overturned the 'inner picture' model of vision. Outside the focus of attention, the world is represented sparsely; the brain stores summary statistics and fetches detail on demand. Vision feels rich because whenever you ask 'what is there?' attention delivers an answer — not because every detail is held in memory. Consciousness is more like a just-in-time service than a continuous recording.

concepts.title: Predictive Coding: From Helmholtz to Friston
concepts.contentHtml:
Hermann von Helmholtz (1867) called perception unconscious inference: the brain combines incoming sensations with prior knowledge to infer the most likely external cause. This idea, dormant for a century, has returned as predictive coding.

On this view (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Karl Friston's free-energy principle, 2005), the cortex is a hierarchy of generative models. Higher layers send predictions down to lower layers; lower layers send prediction errors — the residual unexplained signal — back up. Perception is the configuration of the model that minimises prediction error.

This framework explains many phenomena. Illusions arise when strong priors override weak data. Top-down expectations influence what we perceive: the same blurry word is read differently depending on context. Hallucinations in schizophrenia may reflect over-weighted priors; autism may involve under-weighted priors. The McGurk effect, change blindness, and bistable figures all fit the picture of perception as controlled hallucination constrained by sensory evidence.

Perception, on this account, is not a passive readout of reality. It is the brain's best guess — a hypothesis the senses check.
